newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori mulls reply as MRTA agree to talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori mulls reply as MRTA agree to talks.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori weighed on Thursday his next move in Peru's month-long hostage crisis after Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home agreed to join talks to end the siege.
While accepting a government proposal to set up a "guarantor" commission, rebel leader Nestor Cerpa said on Wednesday his demand that jailed comrades be released must be on the negotiating table.
Fujimori, who has firmly rejected that demand, met for three hours with cabinet colleagues and Japan's ambassador to Mexico to discuss the government's response.
Education Minister Domingo Palermo, the government negotiator who proposed the commission on Sunday, acknowledged receipt of Cerpa's reply in a brief statement.

In a radio conversation from within the residence monitored by Reuters, Cerpa pledged that the rebels would not kill any of their hostages. "It is not in our minds to carry out executions, nor to give any ultimatums," he said.

Despite the apparent breakthrough in the 30-day crisis, the two sides remained far apart on the key issue of the release of about 400 imprisoned Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) members, among them Cerpa's wife.
"The government proposes a peaceful solution but at the same time says it does not have anything to negotiate with us," Cerpa said.

"They ask for a lot of things," Defence Minister Tomas Castillo told reporters. "But what you have to keep in mind is the government's firm position ... that there are no negotiations or concessions."

Japan cautiously welcomed the rebels' communication. "Even if I'm conservative about it, I must say it's not a bad thing. But I would not want to get carried away," said an official of the Japanese government's task force in Lima.

Cerpa warned that without tangible progress in negotiations the crisis was "being pushed towards a military end" and said the government would be to blame for any injury to hostages in a possible storming of the residence.

The rebel leader also told the government his comrades would not accept a peaceful end that amounted to their surrender. "The peaceful way out is not where we go out laying down our arms and giving up," he said. "That is impossible."

Cerpa said the MRTA would accept Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani and a Red Cross representative on the commission as suggested by the government. But the rebels also wanted representation from Guatemala and a European country.

Guatemala's ambassador in Lima Jose Maria Argueta -- himself held hostage at the residence until Dec. 26 -- was standing by to join the talks if called upon by Peru, Foreign Minister Eduardo Stein told reporters in Guatemala City.
Politicians in Lima, who have supported the government's tough line with the rebels, saw the MRTA's decision to join the commission as an important step toward ending the siege.
"It's a positive move and we all have to help as much as we can to reach a happy ending," opposition legislator Antero Florez-Araoz told reporters.

The remaining hostages included two Peruvian ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the younger brother of President Alberto Fujimori.
Captive Foreign Minister Fransisco Tudela said in a brief two-way radio interview with a local television network that the hostages did not have much to say about the latest moves to end the crisis.
"What we observe is that there is a cautious approximation and that is very positive," he said.

In an internet communique, the MRTA called for supporters around the world to join its cause. "It is necessary to put pressure on Fujimori to release all our political prisoner comrades, who are hostages of the dictatorial regime," it said in a statement on its "Rebel Voice" web page.
